text:
Help me write an open letter. I own an independent pharmacy, and I'm writing for 38 independent pharmacies in our state to the state employees' health plan. We'll send it to the plan and to the two newspapers in the capital.

Facts:
- Since January the plan pays us on average $1.80 less per prescription than it costs us to buy and fill it, for the 20 generic drugs we fill most.
- Plan members make up about 22% of the prescriptions at our 38 pharmacies.
- 9 independent pharmacies in the state closed in the last 2 years. We don't know how many closed because of rates.
- In 14 counties, the nearest pharmacy for most people is an independent one.
- The plan's contract with its pharmacy benefit manager comes up for renewal on July 1.
- My own pharmacy filled about 3,100 prescriptions for plan members last year.

I want the letter to say that a third of the independent pharmacies in the state will close within a year if nothing changes. One page.

I'll write the letter once you've answered a few questions. First, here's how I'd build the argument, and one problem with the "a third will close" line that you should decide on before I draft.

**The argument as I see it**

- **Claim:** Before the plan renews its pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) contract on July 1, it should require that pharmacies be paid at least what it costs to buy and fill a prescription.
- **Grounds:** Since January the plan has paid $1.80 less than cost, on average, for the 20 generics we fill most. Plan members are about 22% of our prescriptions. Nine independents have closed in two years. In 14 counties the nearest pharmacy for most people is an independent.
- **Warrant:** A plan that pays below cost for the drugs it covers most is paying for pharmacies to close. When the pharmacy closing is the only one nearby, the plan's own members lose access.
- **Backing:** Your own numbers (3,100 plan prescriptions last year), and whoever has checked the $1.80 figure.
- **Rebuttal the plan will raise:** "The PBM sets those rates, and lower rates keep costs down for the state and its employees."
- **Qualifier:** This depends on your answer below.

**The problem with "a third will close within a year"**

Nothing in your facts supports it yet. You don't say how many independents the state has, so "a third" can't be turned into a number. And the closure record you have is 9 in two years, and you can't say rates caused them. A reporter at either paper will ask "a third of how many, and how do you know?" If the letter can't answer that, the story becomes your number rather than the plan's rates. There are two ways forward:

- **Narrower version, which your facts already support:** "If the July 1 contract renews on these terms, more of us will close. In 14 counties, that leaves plan members with no pharmacy nearby." The July 1 date is a real checkpoint the plan can act on.
- **Keep the bold version** only if you have something behind it. For example, if you surveyed the 38 and a certain number said they can't stay open another year at these rates, the letter can say exactly that, which is stronger than "a third."

It's your call. Tell me which version you want.

**Questions (the first three matter most)**

1. **How many independent pharmacies are in the state now? And have any of the 38 said they'll close or are considering it?** This decides the claim above.
2. **What exactly are you asking the plan to do?** For example, a minimum payment of acquisition cost plus a dispensing fee written into the July 1 contract, PBM pricing transparency, or a meeting before renewal. A specific ask with the date attached makes the letter actionable.
3. **What can you say to "the PBM sets rates, and low rates save taxpayers money"?** Something like evidence the plan pays the PBM more than the PBM pays you, or that members are being steered to mail order, would answer the plan's main objection directly.
4. **What share of your 3,100 plan prescriptions are those 20 generics, and does "cost" in the $1.80 include staff time or only drug cost?** With that, I can state your own pharmacy's yearly loss on plan members. Without it, I can't, because the $1.80 only applies to those 20 drugs.
5. **Who signs, and who is it addressed to?** Your name and pharmacy, whether all 38 are listed, the name and title of the plan's director, and whether to name the PBM.
6. **Is there anything the plan or reporters know, or will find out, that the letter should face head-on?** For example, whether you make money on other plan prescriptions, such as brand-name drugs, or a patient in one of the 14 counties who has already lost a pharmacy nearby.

Once you answer, I'll write the one-page letter.

Go with the narrower version. I can't back up "a third."

1. I don't know how many independents are in the state. None of the 38 have told me they'll close. Two have told me they'll stop filling for plan members if nothing changes.
2. The July 1 renewal should pay at least what the drug costs us, plus a fill fee. I can commit to sharing our purchase invoices for the 20 drugs with the plan, and to meeting the plan's staff any time before May 1.
3. I don't know. I don't have anything on what the plan pays the PBM or on mail order.
4. I don't know the share, and I don't know if the $1.80 includes staff time.
5. Me, Tom Reilly, owner of Reilly Drug in Carver, for the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance. I don't have the director's name or title, or the PBM's name.
6. Some of us make up part of the loss on brand-name drugs. I don't know by how much. Also, in those 14 counties the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away for most people.

I've written the narrower version. The two pharmacies that say they'll stop taking plan members, and the 20-mile distance to the nearest chain, now carry the warning. Both are concrete and checkable, so a reporter can't easily knock them down.

<final_document>
**An open letter to the State Employees' Health Plan**
*From the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance, on behalf of 38 independent pharmacies*

On July 1, the plan's contract with its pharmacy benefit manager comes up for renewal. We ask the plan to use that renewal to make sure pharmacies are paid at least what a drug costs us, plus a fee for filling it.

Since January, for the 20 generic drugs we fill most, the plan has paid us on average $1.80 less per prescription than it costs us to buy and fill it. These are the prescriptions plan members bring us most often. Plan members account for about 22 percent of the prescriptions at our 38 pharmacies. At my own pharmacy, Reilly Drug in Carver, we filled about 3,100 prescriptions for plan members last year.

Some of us make up part of that loss on brand-name drugs, but only part. A pharmacy cannot keep filling its most common prescriptions below cost and count on other drugs to cover the difference.

If the contract renews on these terms, two pharmacies in our alliance have told me they will stop filling prescriptions for plan members. We expect others to follow. Nine independent pharmacies in the state have closed in the last two years. We can't tell you how many of them closed because of rates, and we won't claim they all did. But in 14 counties, the nearest pharmacy for most people is an independent one, and the nearest chain is more than 20 miles away. When a pharmacy there closes or stops taking the plan, plan members in that county don't save money. They drive a round trip of more than 40 miles for a refill.

The plan may say that its pharmacy benefit manager sets these rates. The manager sets them under a contract the plan signs, and on July 1 the plan decides its terms. We are asking the plan to put a floor in that contract: at least the cost of the drug, plus a fill fee.

We don't ask the plan to take our word for our costs. We will share our purchase invoices for these 20 drugs with the plan. We will meet with the plan's staff at any time before May 1, so the plan can check our figures before it signs.

Plan members in 14 counties depend on pharmacies like ours. We want to keep serving them, and we're asking the plan to make that possible.

Tom Reilly
Owner, Reilly Drug, Carver
For the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance
</final_document>

Before you send it, check these:

- **Who it's addressed to:** I used "the State Employees' Health Plan" because I don't have the director's name or the plan's official name. A letter to a named director is harder to ignore, so it's worth looking them up.
- **The invoice offer:** The letter says "we will share our purchase invoices," which reads as the whole alliance. If only Reilly Drug can commit to that, change it to "I will share Reilly Drug's purchase invoices."
- **What I left out because you didn't know it:** your own pharmacy's dollar loss, the size of the brand-name offset, and anything about what the plan pays its benefit manager. If the 38 agree, listing their names under your signature would show the letter really comes from all of them.
